newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders still at odds on employment plan.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders still at odds on employment plan.

text.p: European Union leaders remained at odds on Saturday over how they should battle unemployment in their region, where a jobless total of nearly 18 million is generating growing public insecurity.
Concerned that they may seem unresponsive to European voters' worries, most EU governments want a separate chapter on employment written into the union's Maastricht treaty.
But at an informal summit on the EU's future, Britain and Germany resisted the idea of adding a chapter on employment to the union's Maastricht treaty.
Britain in particular is wedded to the concept of an unfettered labour market and British diplomats said they also had the support of France against an employment chapter.
"The question is a choice between warm words or a treaty chapter," said one British official. "A treaty chapter would be a judicial nightmare."
For example, the diplomats said some might question whether the EU's drive towards economic and monetary union (EMU) would be compatible with obligations on employment.

With a growing public perception that the race for EMU is much to blame for the EU's nearly 11 percent jobless rate, giving the union formal powers to create jobs could offer opponents of a single currency a powerful weapon, diplomats say.
EU governments have been handcuffed in their economic policy options by their efforts to curb budget deficits to qualify for EMU, expected to start in 1999.
But in an attempt to underscore their resolve to tackle the jobs problem, Ireland, the current EU president, said it would issue a declaration on creating jobs in December.
"A declaration on employment adds to the authority of the Union in dealing with this issue," an Irish diplomat said in explaining what Irish prime minister John Bruton told his colleagues.
Such a declaration would give the EU the "philosophical underpinnings" which are seen necessary to unite the 15-nation bloc in its often fractious debate over how to produce more jobs, he added.
"It's more a difference of form than of substantial objectives," added another diplomat in explaining Ireland's position relative to that of Britain's.
Countries like Sweden, Spain and Portugal argue there is broad consensus for giving the EU a more prominent role.
"It seems now that we will be successful when it comes to employment," Swedish prime minister Goran Persson told reporters.
Yet any changes to Maastricht require unanimity, so it is doubtful that a change in the treaty will materialise.
EU leaders also focused on issues including bringing in countries from central and eastern Europe, a common defence and foreign policy, and the political turmoil in the Middle East.
